evergreen.title: Start with Your Soil
evergreen.description: Healthy soil is the foundation of every great garden. Test your soil pH and amend with compost before planting. Most garden plants thrive in slightly acidic to neutral soil (pH 6.0–7.0).

evergreen.title: Water Wisely
evergreen.description: Water deeply and less frequently to encourage deep root growth. Early morning is the best time to water — it reduces evaporation and helps prevent fungal diseases.

evergreen.title: Right Plant, Right Place
evergreen.description: Choose plants that match your site conditions — sun exposure, soil type, and hardiness zone. In Delaware (Zone 7a), you can grow a wide range of perennials, shrubs, and trees.

evergreen.title: Mulch Matters
evergreen.description: Apply 2–3 inches of organic mulch around plants to conserve moisture, suppress weeds, and regulate soil temperature. Keep mulch a few inches away from stems and trunks.

evergreen.title: Feed Your Garden
evergreen.description: Use a balanced fertilizer in spring and supplement with compost throughout the season. Native plants generally need less fertilizer than hybrid varieties.

evergreen.title: Plan for Pollinators
evergreen.description: Include a variety of flower shapes and bloom times to support bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds from early spring through fall. Native wildflowers are especially beneficial.

rhythms.title: Scout for Pests and Disease
rhythms.description: Integrated Pest Management (IPM) relies heavily on early detection. Regularly inspecting the undersides of leaves, stems, and soil helps catch outbreaks—like aphids or fungal spores—before they spread. Early intervention allows for mechanical controls (like hand-picking or a blast of water) rather than chemical interventions.

rhythms.title: Stay Ahead of the Weeds
rhythms.description: Weeds aggressively compete with desired plants for water, soil nutrients, and sunlight. Removing them when they are small prevents them from establishing deep taproots or setting seed, which exponentially reduces future weed pressure in the garden bed.

rhythms.title: Deadhead for Continuous Blooms
rhythms.frequency: Weekly to Bi-weekly (during the growing season)
rhythms.description: When flowers fade and begin to set seed, hormonal signals direct the plant's energy into reproduction. Removing spent blooms (deadheading) interrupts this process, redirecting energy back into vegetative growth and the production of new flower buds.

rhythms.title: Harvest Often to Encourage Yields
rhythms.description: For fruiting plants like beans, cucumbers, and tomatoes, leaving mature fruit on the vine signals to the plant that its reproductive cycle is complete, slowing further flowering. Frequent harvesting keeps the plant in active production and ensures produce is picked at peak flavor.

rhythms.title: Tend Your Compost Pile
rhythms.description: An active, hot compost pile requires oxygen to support the aerobic bacteria responsible for rapid decomposition. Turning the pile regularly and maintaining an even moisture level speeds up the breakdown of organic matter and prevents the anaerobic conditions that cause foul odors.

rhythms.title: Clean and Maintain Your Tools
rhythms.frequency: Monthly (and immediately after pruning diseased plants)
rhythms.description: Dull blades crush plant stems rather than making clean cuts, leaving jagged wounds that are highly vulnerable to pathogens. Additionally, sap and dirt on tools can harbor and transmit soil-borne bacterial and fungal diseases between plants. Regular cleaning, oiling, and sharpening protect the garden's overall health.
